aiProducts.title: Enterprise Product & Delivery Playbook
aiProducts.subtitle: Evolving enterprise product · Web platform foundation verified · Working proof of concept
aiProducts.imageAlt: Playbook proof of concept: six phase cards, each showing its gate decision and open conditions (fictional example data)
aiProducts.summary: An enterprise product for guiding AI, non-AI and hybrid initiatives that I created and lead. It grew from my enterprise experience, graduate study in Enterprise AI and the Enterprise AI Blueprint into a six-phase, 18-step methodology, a working proof of concept and a web platform whose foundation has been verified locally with synthetic data. I defined its vision, requirements, roadmap, governance framework and acceptance criteria, and I use AI coding assistance for implementation.
capabilities: Product vision and strategy: one governed lifecycle for AI, non-AI and hybrid initiatives
Requirements under change control and a milestone roadmap tied to user outcomes
Prioritization: governance, security and data isolation before workflow features
Decision traceability: every gate decision records who decided, why and under what conditions
Validation and acceptance: each milestone accepted against criteria I define
aiProducts.businessProblem: Product Managers often rely on multiple tools, documents and spreadsheets to manage requirements, decisions, risks, evidence and delivery progress. This can make it difficult to maintain consistent delivery practices, understand why decisions were made and provide leadership with a reliable view of initiative progress. I created the Playbook to address this problem while complementing existing enterprise systems and governance processes.
aiProducts.productVision: My vision is to provide Product Managers and their teams with a consistent, repeatable approach to guiding AI, non-AI and hybrid initiatives from business problem through requirements, design, delivery, adoption and ongoing operation. The platform is designed to support configurable guidance, governance, risk management, decision traceability and executive visibility. Planned AI assistance and controlled agentic execution would operate within defined boundaries while people retain oversight and accountability.
aiProducts.technicalArchitecture: One modular web application with a separate workspace for each organization, role-based access and an append-only audit history, verified locally with synthetic data and not yet deployed. It is designed to run locally or be self-hosted, with no mandatory paid services, and integrations stay optional. Self-hosted deployment has not been implemented or verified. The original proof of concept is a local, single-user application.
keyFeatures: Working proof of concept: all 18 steps and six gated phase reviews, decisions with conditions, risk and evidence registers, and reassessment when answers change

Implemented and verified locally with synthetic data (Milestones 1–2): organization isolation, roles and append-only audit history; several product managers per initiative; protected evidence; an executive rollup limited to what each viewer may see
In planning (Milestone 3): the proposed objective is to bring the six-phase, 18-step lifecycle into the web platform. Scope and implementation are not yet authorized

Product vision (planned): intake and solution suitability, configurable questions and stakeholder guidance, regulatory applicability, responsible AI and controlled agentic execution, departmental AI readiness and adoption, and value realization through SQDC
Planned (proposed roadmap): organization tailoring, pilot and value tracking, operational review, optional integrations and enterprise release readiness
businessValue: Safety: mandatory controls and a named accountable owner before work proceeds
Quality: decisions tied to reviewed evidence, with history preserved
Delivery: clear next actions and less repeated data entry
Cost: pilots and value reviews that show whether outcomes justify investment
aiProducts.blueprintConnection: The Playbook is one of several independently operable products in the Enterprise AI Platform Program, alongside PortfolioIQ (working prototype) and a proposed Leadership Dashboard (in discovery). Each product is designed to operate independently. Optional integration through defined interfaces is the planned architectural direction and is not yet implemented.

aiProducts.title: PortfolioIQ
aiProducts.subtitle: Working prototype · Public demo on sample data
aiProducts.summary: A working prototype I created to explore how structured evaluation criteria, automated recommendations and AI-assisted analysis could support application portfolio decisions. A rules-based scoring engine generates explainable retain, modernize, retire or replace recommendations. Claude answers questions about the portfolio but does not determine recommendations, and people review recommendations and make the final decisions, with written rationale required for overrides. I defined the product vision, requirements, architectural direction, governance requirements and acceptance criteria, and used AI coding assistance for implementation.
capabilities: Explainable rules-based recommendation engine: eight supporting signals displayed per application, some applied directly by the decision rules and others indirectly through the technical debt score
Recommendation confidence and review guidance (Inside, Edge or Outside), derived from rules-based scoring and not calibrated as a measure of recommendation reliability
Human oversight and decision governance: people review recommendations and make the final decisions, with written rationale required for overrides
Recommendation drift indicator (simulated in the prototype, not operational monitoring)
Conversational portfolio analysis with Claude, which receives the portfolio data directly and does not determine recommendations
Session query limit and shared passphrase for the AI screen, used as prototype cost controls rather than production security controls
ServiceNow Table API connector with automatic CSV fallback (the public demo runs on sample CSV data)
businessValue: Intended to help Application Portfolio Managers evaluate applications using consistent, explainable criteria
Intended to reduce manual analysis while preserving human accountability for portfolio decisions
Demonstrates the recommendation, review and decision recording workflow through a working public prototype
aiProducts.businessProblem: Application Portfolio Managers need to make informed decisions about which applications to retain, modernize, retire or replace. In large enterprise portfolios, these decisions can be difficult when information is spread across multiple systems and evaluation criteria are inconsistent.
aiProducts.productVision: The opportunity was to bring the governance discipline of my GE Vernova Application Portfolio Management dashboard to an AI-assisted version, where automation accelerates the recommendation without removing human accountability for the decision. The problem also reflects my predictive maintenance work, where I reviewed the available application portfolio information to check whether an existing application could meet the business requirements. I didn't find an equivalent, but limited visibility into the broader enterprise portfolio meant I couldn't confirm that across the enterprise.
aiProducts.technicalArchitecture: A decision-support architecture in which portfolio data feeds a deterministic, rules-based scoring and recommendation layer. Every recommendation is explainable and can be reviewed in a human review queue, and reviewed decisions are recorded in a session-based audit log with CSV export. Claude provides conversational analysis over the same data and does not set recommendations.
keyFeatures: Six-screen guided workflow from portfolio overview to a reviewed, exportable decision
Approve, override or escalate recommendations in the review queue, with written rationale required for overrides
Session query limit to manage API cost in the public demo
Session-based decision audit log with CSV export for stakeholder and leadership review
aiProducts.blueprintConnection: PortfolioIQ is the application portfolio assessment product of the Enterprise AI Platform Program, alongside the Enterprise Product & Delivery Playbook and a proposed Leadership Dashboard (in discovery). Each product is designed to operate independently. Integration through defined interfaces, such as PortfolioIQ assessments informing Playbook decisions, is a planned architectural direction and isn't implemented. Further investment depends on validated demand.

enterpriseProjects.title: Engineering Knowledge Database Replacement
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Product ownership, requirements discovery and phased delivery
enterpriseProjects.challenge: Lotus Notes was being retired, putting years of engineering documentation and procedures for boiler design at risk and raising the risk of engineers relying on outdated information.
outcomes: Migrated documentation for approximately five engineering departments while preserving years of engineering knowledge
Participating departments moved to the new solution and used it after migration and training
Avoided purchasing a replacement platform by using the existing SharePoint environment, with a third-party tool purchased for the migration
Improved metadata quality by correcting outdated metadata during the migration
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: A retiring Lotus Notes application put access to years of engineering knowledge and documentation at risk. I met with department leaders to understand their requirements and determined that our existing SharePoint platform could meet their needs without purchasing another platform, which also suited engineers who already knew SharePoint. I took a phased approach, starting with a smaller engineering department before expanding the migration. We used a third-party migration tool to transfer the documentation and remap its metadata, correcting outdated metadata along the way. When an engineer requested an enhancement to the retiring application, I deferred the request to the replacement application's backlog rather than invest further in the legacy system. Based on early user feedback, we added a week of hands-on lunchtime workshops to support adoption. Documentation for approximately five engineering departments was migrated, and the participating departments moved to the new solution and used it.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: Engineering departments depended on years of accumulated documentation and procedures supporting boiler design. The retirement of Lotus Notes created a business continuity risk and a risk that engineers would rely on outdated information.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I worked directly with department leaders and engineers to understand their business needs and define requirements. I owned the platform selection and rollout strategy, led the migration and prepared users for the transition. I also managed requirements prioritization and adjusted our approach based on user feedback.
keyContributions: Met with department leaders to understand their requirements.
Evaluated existing enterprise capabilities before considering a new platform, and selected SharePoint because it met the requirements and engineers already knew it.
Started with a smaller engineering department, then expanded the migration.
Used a third-party migration tool and process to transfer documentation, remap metadata and correct outdated metadata.
Deferred an engineer's enhancement request for the retiring application to the replacement application's backlog.
Added a week of hands-on lunchtime workshops after early user feedback.
enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: This experience helped shape my approach to adoption and change enablement within the Enterprise AI Blueprint. Delivering a technically sound solution is only part of the responsibility. We also need to prepare users, listen to their feedback and adjust our approach to support adoption.

enterpriseProjects.title: Boiler Performance Tools Modernization
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Technical Product Owner & Scrum Master
enterpriseProjects.challenge: Multiple engineering departments depended on about 20 custom FORTRAN applications for boiler design that ran on aging, unsupported technology, and the business needed to protect software it licensed externally.
outcomes: Multiple modernized applications were deployed to AWS, and engineers began using them
Preserved engineering capabilities supporting legacy boiler design while reducing dependency on unsupported technology
Established an engineering validation approach that reused existing test cases to confirm equivalent calculation results
Addressed intellectual property protection requirements for externally licensed engineering software
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: Multiple engineering departments depended on about 20 custom FORTRAN applications for boiler design that ran on aging, unsupported technology, and the business also needed to protect software it licensed externally. As Product Owner and Scrum Master, I led the team responsible for modernizing this portfolio of applications using C# and AWS, retaining legacy components where appropriate. I worked with engineering stakeholders and software engineers to set modernization priorities, starting with the applications needed for upcoming engineering projects. When engineers found that some modules couldn't be converted directly to C#, they designed a wrapper around the existing FORTRAN code, and I replaced the original story, had the team size the new work and adjusted the sprint plan. I worked with engineering application owners to repurpose their existing test cases so we could confirm the modernized applications produced equivalent calculation results. Multiple modernized applications were deployed to AWS, engineers began using them, and intellectual property protection requirements were addressed.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: Multiple engineering departments depended on custom legacy applications for boiler design and engineering work. The applications relied on aging FORTRAN software and unsupported infrastructure, so the business needed to preserve these engineering capabilities while moving to a more supportable technology environment. Protecting the intellectual property in externally licensed engineering software was also a consideration.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I owned requirements, backlog prioritization, sprint planning and coordination of business validation, and I ran the Scrum ceremonies. The software engineers and solution architect owned the technical design and implementation, including the FORTRAN wrapper. The cloud engineering team provisioned the AWS environment.
keyContributions: Worked with engineering stakeholders and software engineers to set modernization priorities, starting with the applications needed for upcoming engineering projects.
Defined requirements and user stories with business stakeholders and the solution architect.
Worked with engineering to redefine the blocked conversion work as wrapper work and adjusted the sprint plan.
Worked with engineering application owners to repurpose existing test cases to confirm equivalent calculation results.
Supported requirements for protecting proprietary engineering software.

enterpriseProjects.title: Application Portfolio Management
enterpriseProjects.role: Senior Staff Technical Program Manager · Assignment: Application Portfolio Management Lead
enterpriseProjects.challenge: The Steam business needed to improve application portfolio governance, and leadership had to request portfolio information from the portfolio manager rather than see it directly.
outcomes: Worked with application owners and technical teams to approximately double portfolio health scores within two quarters and meet the centrally established governance targets for critical and noncritical applications
Worked with the teams responsible for the divestiture to ensure the application portfolio accurately reflected organizational and application changes
Gave the Steam CIO and IT directors self-service portfolio visibility, and the dashboard became the basis for quarterly governance discussions
Coordinated the retirement of approximately 50 applications through rationalization outside the divestiture, with application owners making the final decisions
Established a recurring governance process that prompted remediation and retirement by application owners and technical teams, though some individual applications still had open issues
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: When I took over application portfolio management for the Steam business, leadership needed better governance performance and had to request portfolio information rather than see it directly. I worked with the central governance team to understand the portfolio health metrics, worked with the CIO and directors to understand their reporting needs, and built a centralized Smartsheet dashboard from the enterprise source system covering portfolio health, technical debt, metadata completeness, application footprint, hosting and retirement progress. I worked with application owners in quarterly reviews to identify retirement opportunities and coordinate application rationalization while owners kept the final decision, reported progress to leadership monthly and ran quarterly governance reviews with the Steam CIO and domain directors. Working with application owners and technical teams, we approximately doubled portfolio health scores within two quarters and met the centrally established targets, though some individual applications still had open issues. Over my ownership the portfolio went from about 300 to about 100 applications. About three quarters of that reduction came from a divestiture, and I worked with the teams responsible for it to maintain an accurate application portfolio. Separately, about 50 applications were retired through rationalization.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: The Steam business needed to improve application portfolio governance performance while giving leadership better visibility into portfolio health, composition and application retirement progress. Leadership previously had to request this information from the application portfolio manager.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I worked with the CIO and directors to understand what information they needed to manage the application portfolio. I defined the dashboard requirements, built the Smartsheet tracking and reporting solution, worked with application owners to address information gaps and coordinated remediation activities with the responsible technical teams. I also led quarterly portfolio reviews to help leadership understand application health, technical debt, hosting, modernization opportunities and decommissioning candidates. The governance scoring methodology was defined centrally, and I didn't design it. Application owners kept the final decision on retiring their applications. I worked with the teams responsible for the divestiture to maintain an accurate application portfolio.
keyContributions: Worked with the central governance team to understand the portfolio health metrics and requirements.
Worked with the CIO and directors to understand their reporting and governance needs.
Built a centralized Smartsheet dashboard from the enterprise source system covering portfolio health, technical debt, metadata completeness, application footprint, hosting and retirement progress.
Worked with application owners in quarterly reviews to identify retirement opportunities and coordinate application rationalization, while owners kept the final decision.
Reported progress to leadership monthly and ran quarterly governance reviews with the Steam CIO and domain directors.
Worked with the teams responsible for the divestiture to ensure the application portfolio accurately reflected the changes.
enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: This connects to the Blueprint's starting point, which is agreeing on what leaders need to decide before building the reporting or the model.

enterpriseProjects.title: Predictive-Maintenance Application: AWS Deployment
enterpriseProjects.role: Senior Staff Technical Program Manager · Assignment: Technical Product Manager
enterpriseProjects.challenge: A purchased predictive maintenance application needed to be brought into production so service engineers could analyze customer equipment data and recommend preventive maintenance.
outcomes: Turned previously purchased software into an operational capability that service engineers could use to analyze vibration data and identify potential equipment failures
Service engineers began using the application following deployment and training
Trained three service engineers and gave them reusable documentation and video training so they could train other engineers
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: With support from my leadership and the responsible Domain Director, I took ownership of bringing a purchased predictive maintenance application into service on AWS so service engineers could use it to support customers. It analyzes vibration data from customer equipment to identify potential failures and recommend preventive maintenance. I worked with service engineers to understand the business problem and intended value, and I reviewed the available application portfolio information to check whether an existing application already provided similar functionality. I coordinated GE's standard onboarding process with enterprise architecture, security, cloud engineering and the vendor, and personally installed and configured the application on AWS. I created documentation and a video walkthrough, personally trained three service engineers and gave them reusable training resources so they could train others. An existing software investment became an operational capability that service engineers began using.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: Service engineers needed a way to predict potential equipment failures and recommend preventive maintenance for customers. The purchased application could do this, but it had to be onboarded, installed, and put into use first.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: With support from my leadership and the responsible Domain Director, I owned bringing the application into service. I worked with the service engineers on their needs, coordinated onboarding with enterprise architecture, security, cloud engineering and the vendor, personally installed and configured the application, and trained the users. The cloud engineering team provisioned and configured the AWS environment.
keyContributions: Worked directly with service engineers to understand their business needs and the decisions they wanted to support.
Reviewed the available application portfolio information to check whether an existing application provided similar functionality.
Coordinated the standard enterprise onboarding process with enterprise architecture, security, cloud engineering and the vendor.
Coordinated architecture and security requirements and approvals before go-live.
Worked directly with the vendor on installation requirements and personally installed and configured the application on AWS.
Created documentation and a video walkthrough, personally trained three service engineers and equipped them to train others.
enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: Buying technology and putting it into service are different steps. The Blueprint treats that handoff as part of the plan for AI initiatives.

enterpriseProjects.title: U.S. Steam Tendering Application
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Requirements, backlog, and platform recommendation
enterpriseProjects.challenge: The tendering team relied on a file share that made it hard to find documents, tell which version was current, know who owned a document and manage approvals. An IT director proposed using Box.
outcomes: The tendering team moved from the file share to SharePoint and used it
Users could search document contents rather than relying only on filenames and folders
Improved document ownership, version control and approvals through structured metadata and approval workflows
The platform was chosen to fit the required workflow, with agreement from the IT and Tendering directors
Kept product ownership after launch and delivered enhancements as business needs changed
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: The U.S. Steam tendering team relied on a file share that made it hard to find documents, tell which version was current, know who owned a document and manage approvals. I worked with the team to understand these problems and defined requirements for document ownership, metadata, version control, approval workflows and information discovery. An IT director proposed using Box. I compared what each platform could do against the workflow the team needed and recommended SharePoint because it was the better fit, and the IT and Tendering directors agreed to proceed with it. Using existing SharePoint capabilities, I implemented structured metadata, document ownership, version control and approval workflows, and enabled full-text search of document contents. The team moved from the file share to SharePoint, and I kept product ownership after launch, delivering enhancements as business needs changed.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: The file share's folder structure made it difficult to locate relevant documents, determine current versions, identify document owners and manage approvals.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I owned the requirements, the backlog, the working versions of the application and the platform recommendation, and I kept product ownership after launch.
keyContributions: Worked with the tendering team to understand their business problems, decisions and intended value.
Defined requirements for document ownership, metadata, version control, approval workflows and information discovery.
Compared Box and SharePoint against the team's required workflow and recommended SharePoint as the better fit.
Implemented structured metadata, document ownership, version control, approval workflows and full-text search using existing SharePoint capabilities.
Kept product ownership after launch and delivered enhancements as business needs changed.

enterpriseProjects.title: ME Intranet Migration Recovery
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Recovery plan, schedule, and delivery
enterpriseProjects.challenge: A business unit's move from an outdated intranet to SharePoint had stalled, and that unit's confidence in IT was low.
outcomes: Recovered a stalled migration and delivered on the date set during the recovery
Completed under the original budget, with about $43K in reported savings
Improved the business unit's working relationship with IT
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: When I joined Pratt & Whitney, the ME business unit's migration from an outdated intranet to SharePoint had stalled. The application owner was trying to manage it without the IT support they needed, and the IT services vendor was committed elsewhere. I met with the application owner and business stakeholders to understand their pain points and what they needed from the new intranet. I broke the remaining work into tasks with owners and estimates, built the schedule in Microsoft Project, and set a delivery date. I explained the business impact to the vendor's director, secured commitments for development and data migration, and ran weekly progress meetings. The migration was completed by that date and under the original budget, with about $43K in reported savings, and the working relationship with the business unit improved.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: The business unit had been waiting on a stalled migration, and the vendor's team was committed to other work.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I owned the recovery, including the plan, the schedule and delivery date, the resource commitments, and progress tracking. SharePoint had already been selected. I didn't manage the original budget, and the savings were reported against it.
keyContributions: Met with the application owner and stakeholders to understand their pain points and needs.
Built a Microsoft Project schedule from task-owner estimates and set the delivery date.
Secured vendor commitments and ran weekly progress meetings.

enterpriseProjects.title: Steam IT PMO
enterpriseProjects.role: Senior Staff Technical Program Manager · Assignment: Program Manager / PMO Lead
enterpriseProjects.challenge: The Steam CIO could see larger initiatives, but getting information on smaller projects managed within individual domains meant contacting each domain director.
outcomes: Centralized approximately 100 project requests through one intake process over the life of the PMO
Gave leadership visibility into approximately 10 concurrent projects, with schedule and budget risks surfaced for discussion
Gave the CIO self-service visibility into project performance across domains
Established a consistent process for leadership to approve, reject or postpone project requests
Established consistent project management and reporting practices, supported by documentation and direct training
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: The Steam CIO could see larger initiatives but had no central view of smaller projects managed within individual domains, and getting project information meant contacting each domain director. I set up a lightweight PMO in Smartsheet, customizing an existing template to fit the business requirements. I established a central project request and intake process, defined the information each request needed, and brought request reviews into quarterly leadership meetings, where leadership could approve, reject or postpone requests pending more information. I set up a standard project lifecycle structure, built an executive dashboard showing progress, schedule risk, budget risk and completion, and trained the designated project managers using documentation I wrote. Some wanted to keep their own spreadsheets, so I let them use those day to day but kept Smartsheet as the single source for reporting. Over the life of the PMO, about 100 project requests came through the central intake, and leadership could see about 10 concurrent projects.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: The CIO had visibility into larger initiatives but not into smaller projects managed independently within individual domains, and getting project information required contacting each domain director.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I designed and ran the PMO intake and reporting process. The Project Managers reported to their Domain Directors, not to me, so adoption depended on influence rather than authority. I surfaced project health, while each project's manager owned its delivery and any recovery plan.
keyContributions: Set up a lightweight PMO in Smartsheet, customizing an existing template to fit the business requirements.
Established a central project request and intake process and defined the information each request needed.
Brought project request reviews into quarterly leadership meetings, where leadership approved, rejected or postponed requests.
Built an executive dashboard showing project progress, schedule and budget risks, and completion.
Wrote training documentation with screenshots and trained the designated project managers.
enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: This connects to the Blueprint's view that the operating model and adoption have to be planned together, not one after the other.

enterpriseProjects.title: SharePoint Upgrade: The No-Go Decision
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Cutover planning and go/no-go decision
enterpriseProjects.challenge: Engineering's SharePoint environment had to be upgraded to a version supported by the data center.
outcomes: Avoided relying on potentially incomplete data after the old environment was restarted
The second cutover had no reported post-launch data-integrity issues
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: Engineering's SharePoint project-execution environment had to move to a 64-bit version supported by the data center. During the cutover, the old environment was restarted, which meant data could diverge between the old and new systems. I made the no-go decision and accepted the delay. I took ownership of the unclear shutdown instructions that had allowed the restart, reset responsibilities and checkpoints, and validated the migration before retrying. The second cutover had no reported post-launch data-integrity issues.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: The platform supported engineering's project execution, so the upgrade could not risk losing data.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I made the no-go decision and owned the reset, with clearer responsibilities and checkpoints and validation before the second cutover. I also took ownership of the unclear shutdown instructions that contributed to the restart.
keyContributions: Stopped the cutover when the old environment was restarted, accepting the schedule delay.
Took ownership of the unclear shutdown instructions and reset responsibilities and checkpoints.
Validated the migration before the second cutover.
enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: This connects to the Blueprint's view that governance must include the authority to stop, even when it costs schedule.

enterpriseProjects.title: Document Data Quality Improvement
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Metadata correction process and owner coordination
enterpriseProjects.challenge: A long-standing SharePoint metadata issue had gone unresolved while developer capacity was unavailable.
outcomes: Resolved a metadata issue that had gone unresolved for over a year
Document owners validated the corrections to their own data
Resolved the issue using existing tools without requiring custom development
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: A SharePoint metadata problem had gone unresolved for over a year while developer capacity was unavailable. I used a third-party tool to export the metadata into department-specific Excel files, had document owners validate the corrections, and reimported it. That resolved the issue without custom development.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: The issue had remained unresolved for over a year because developer capacity was not available.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I designed the correction process and coordinated the document owners, who validated the corrections to their own data.
keyContributions: Exported the metadata into department-specific Excel files using a third-party tool.
Had document owners validate the corrections.
Reimported the corrected metadata without custom development.
enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: This connects to the Blueprint's view that governance needs clear data ownership, not just process.

enterpriseProjects.title: ITAR/EAR Collaboration Templates
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Technical Product Manager / SharePoint Governance Lead
enterpriseProjects.challenge: Regulated engineering data needed SharePoint collaboration that supported ITAR and EAR export-control requirements and still worked for engineering teams.
outcomes: SharePoint collaboration templates for regulated engineering sites, developed with vendors to support ITAR and EAR requirements
Export logging and scanning controls for regulated sites, developed with vendors and IT, security, legal, and compliance partners
enterpriseProjects.executiveSummary: At Pratt & Whitney, I supported SharePoint governance for sites handling export-controlled engineering information. I collaborated with vendors and internal IT, security, legal, and compliance stakeholders on collaboration templates and export logging and scanning controls designed to support ITAR and EAR requirements.
enterpriseProjects.businessChallenge: Export-control requirements are strict, and the controls also had to fit how engineering teams collaborate day to day.
enterpriseProjects.myRole: I led SharePoint governance for these sites and collaborated with vendors on the collaboration templates and controls.
keyContributions: Collaborated with vendors on SharePoint collaboration templates supporting ITAR and EAR requirements.
Collaborated with vendors on export logging and scanning controls for regulated sites.
Worked with IT, security, legal, and compliance partners on SharePoint governance for regulated sites.
enterpriseProjects.blueprintConnection: This experience reinforced the importance of working with security, legal, compliance and business stakeholders to establish governance controls that support both regulatory requirements and operational needs.

enterpriseProjects.title: Agile Introduction
enterpriseProjects.role: Assignment: Agile introduction, training, and Scrum facilitation

enterpriseProjects.myRole: At the director's request, I introduced Agile to the team, trained the developers, facilitated the Scrum ceremonies, and coached them through adoption.

Trained the developers and facilitated Scrum ceremonies.
Coached the team through adoption.

hero.headline: Enterprise product leadership, with AI as a differentiator.
narrative: I'm an enterprise product and technology leader who enjoys working directly with business and technical teams to solve problems, improve operations and deliver products that provide measurable value.
I understand the broader enterprise environment and how to leverage its capabilities to support the needs of individual departments and business functions.

whyAI.label: WHY ENTERPRISE AI
whyAI.headline: The hardest problems were never really about the technology.
body: My experience managing enterprise products and technology initiatives helped me recognize that delivering business value requires more than implementing technology. It requires understanding business needs, establishing clear ownership, managing risks and preparing people to adopt new ways of working.

I pursued graduate education in Enterprise AI to build on that experience and better understand how organizations can apply AI responsibly and effectively. I brought my professional experience and education together to develop the Enterprise AI Blueprint and the products that put these principles into practice.

blueprint.label: STRUCTURED METHODOLOGY
blueprint.headline: The Enterprise AI Blueprint
body: The Enterprise AI Blueprint is a structured methodology I developed to help organizations and individual departments understand their current state, assess AI readiness, identify capability gaps, establish or leverage existing operating models and connect AI initiatives to measurable business outcomes.

It recognizes that departments may have different business needs, priorities, resources and levels of AI readiness. The methodology helps teams operationalize AI while working within existing enterprise strategies, technology platforms and governance policies.
It draws on my enterprise technology leadership experience, recent applied AI product work and focused research into how organizations move AI from experimentation to sustained enterprise capability.

hero.headline: The Enterprise AI Blueprint
body: The Enterprise AI Blueprint is a structured methodology that organizations and individual departments can use to move AI from isolated pilots to a governed, measurable business capability.

The Enterprise AI Blueprint emerged from a simple observation. The organizational disciplines that determine whether enterprise technology succeeds also determine whether Enterprise AI succeeds. Governance, product leadership, operating models, adoption, and value realization are not AI-specific. They are enterprise capabilities that become even more critical as organizations operationalize AI.

Departments have different business needs, priorities, resources and levels of AI readiness. A department doesn't need to redesign the organization's operating model to use the Blueprint. It can build on existing enterprise strategy, approved technology platforms, governance policies and supporting teams.
That perspective was shaped by my experience leading enterprise technology investment, governance and product management at GE Vernova, GE Power, Pratt & Whitney and Alstom.

struggle.label: WHY ORGANIZATIONS STRUGGLE
struggle.headline: A successful pilot is only the beginning. Building the governance, operating model and organizational capabilities to sustain AI as an enterprise capability is the harder work.
struggle.intro: A pilot can be funded and demonstrated on its own. What's difficult is everything after the demo, including governance that holds up under real use, delivery that survives contact with existing systems, adoption that outlasts the initial enthusiasm, and a way to prove the investment was worth it. Selecting the right technology is only part of the challenge. Organizations must also establish the governance, delivery and adoption capabilities required to operate AI at scale.

patterns.title: Treated as a project, not a capability
patterns.body: The pilot succeeds, then ends, because there was never a plan to operate it as an ongoing part of the business.

patterns.title: Governance added after the fact
patterns.body: Oversight gets bolted on once something goes wrong, instead of being designed into the initiative from the start.

patterns.title: Adoption left to chance
patterns.body: The tool is deployed, but no one owns whether people actually change how they work because of it.

steps.label: THE SIX-STEP BLUEPRINT
steps.headline: A structured path from fragmented activity to operational AI capability.
steps.intro: Each step answers a specific leadership question. Together, they move an organization or department from uncertainty about where it stands to a governed capability it can measure and sustain.

howItWorks.label: HOW THE BLUEPRINT WORKS
howItWorks.headline: Each phase builds on the one before it.
body: The Blueprint is sequential, not because process demands it, but because each phase produces something the next phase depends on. You cannot design a credible operating model before you understand your actual readiness. You cannot operationalize AI at scale on top of a governance structure that doesn't yet exist.

In practice, the phases are iterative. Organizations revisit earlier phases as conditions change, new initiatives emerge, or readiness gaps close. What stays constant is the discipline of not skipping ahead. When a later-stage concern such as adoption or governance isn't addressed at the stage where it's needed, it becomes harder to resolve later.

operatingModel.heading: Step 04 in Detail: The Enterprise AI Operating Model
operatingModel.intro: Step 04 defines the Enterprise AI Operating Model. The Blueprint's six steps describe how an organization or department moves forward, and the Operating Model's six capability domains describe what must be owned and sustained. They don't happen in sequence. Each needs clear ownership, they operate continuously, and decisions in one domain shape the others. A department doesn't have to build every domain itself. It can rely on enterprise strategy, approved platforms, governance policies and supporting teams that already exist. Readiness is assessed earlier, in Step 2.

domains.name: Strategy & Portfolio Management
domains.question: What AI initiatives should we pursue, and why?
domains.does: It selects and prioritizes AI initiatives against business strategy and manages them as a portfolio.
domains.why: Investment goes to the initiatives most likely to create value, and strategy shapes how the other domains are governed and delivered.

domains.name: AI Platform & Technology Strategy
domains.question: What enterprise AI platform, architecture, model and integration capabilities are required?
domains.does: It defines the shared platform, architecture, models and integrations that initiatives build on.
domains.why: Initiatives build on consistent, supportable foundations instead of solving the same technology problems separately.

domains.name: AI Delivery & Product Management
domains.question: How do we consistently deliver enterprise AI capabilities?
domains.does: It turns approved initiatives into working capabilities through product management and a governed delivery lifecycle.
domains.why: Consistent delivery is how strategy becomes something the business can use, and it shapes adoption.

domains.name: AI Governance
domains.question: How do we govern AI responsibly throughout its lifecycle?
domains.does: It establishes oversight, human accountability, decision rights and risk management across the AI lifecycle, drawing on established risk and compliance frameworks. Oversight is matched to the risk and intended use, from AI that supports human decisions to bounded automation of approved tasks.
domains.why: Governance designed in from the start lets AI scale with trust.

domains.name: Adoption & Change Enablement
domains.question: How do we ensure people successfully adopt AI?
domains.does: It prepares people and supports changes to workflows through training, communication and ongoing support.
domains.why: Value depends on people actually changing how they work.

domains.name: Value Realization & Performance Management
domains.question: How do we measure, sustain and improve business value?
domains.does: It defines how value is measured, tracks results and feeds what's learned back into priorities.
domains.why: Business outcomes are the feedback that keeps the whole model improving.

principles.label: PRODUCT THINKING
principles.headline: Five principles behind how these get built.

items.title: Start With the Decision
items.body: Define what needs to be decided, who owns it, and what success looks like before any model gets involved.

items.title: Separate Pattern From Judgment
items.body: AI supports pattern recognition. Humans own the tradeoffs and the accountability.

items.title: Match Oversight to Risk
items.body: Human oversight should fit the risk and intended use. In PortfolioIQ, the rules engine recommends, and a person reviews recommendations and makes the final decision.

items.title: Track What Goes Wrong
items.body: False positives, false negatives, and business impact should be measured, not assumed. PortfolioIQ records recommendation overrides, and formal error measurement is planned.

items.title: Assign Ownership
items.body: Every capability has a named owner and a feedback loop that keeps it honest over time.
